tagline: Silver-mine tramways, clay spires and a railroad depot along US 93.
intro: US 93 crosses Meadow Valley between Panaca and Caliente, then bends west through mountainous terrain toward Crystal Springs. The stretch between US 6/50 and State Route 318 is a Nevada Scenic Byway. Near Panaca, Cathedral Gorge adds a landscape of clay spires and cave-like formations; Nevada State Parks identifies erosion in soft bentonite clay as their sculptor.

This road carried a state number before it carried a U.S. shield. When US 93 was established in 1926, its southern end was at Wells, Nevada. The later extension brought the national route through the existing state-road network south of that original terminus. In 1931, the American Association of State Highway Officials approved extending US 93 south from Wells to Glendale. By 1932, Nevada had marked the extension over existing state highways, including State Route 7 through Pioche, Caliente and Crystal Springs. The entire Nevada portion of US 93 was paved by 1939.

Heading south from US 6/50, the journey reaches Pioche, whose town center lies west of the highway. Continue toward Cathedral Gorge and the turnoff for Panaca, then through Meadow Valley to Caliente. From Caliente, US 93 turns west toward the junction with State Routes 318 and 375 near Crystal Springs.

moments.title: Pioche
moments.text: Ore buckets remain suspended above parts of Pioche, on the cables of an abandoned aerial tramway. During the 1920s and 1930s, the tram carried silver and nickel ore from the mines to the Godbe Mill. Mining had already made Pioche an important Nevada silver town by the early 1870s. The town also retains two neighboring theaters above downtown: Thompson’s Opera House, built in 1873 and restored in 2009, and the Gem Theater, built in 1937. US 93 bypasses the center to the east, with State Routes 321 and 322 providing direct access to town.
moments.notice: Tramway cables cross parts of town with some original ore buckets intact.

moments.title: Cathedral Gorge State Park
moments.text: Cathedral Gorge’s spires began with volcanic ash deposited in layers hundreds of feet thick. Erosion shaped the soft bentonite clay into the narrow valley’s spires and cave-like forms. In the 1920s, the formations served as a backdrop for outdoor plays and annual Easter ceremonies. Governor James Scrugham set the area aside for preservation in 1924, and it became one of Nevada’s first four state parks in 1935. Walking trails enter the formations, while a one-mile trail links Miller Point overlook with the picnic area. Civilian Conservation Corps picnic facilities remain in use, while its stone water tower and restroom no longer operate.
moments.notice: Look for the buff-colored cliffs and spires carved from soft clay.

moments.title: Caliente
moments.text: Caliente’s 1923 depot served a railroad division point where locomotives received maintenance and helper engines were based. The Mission Revival building had passenger and railroad offices downstairs and a hotel upstairs. Diesel locomotives reduced the railroad’s need for Caliente; locomotive maintenance moved to Las Vegas in 1948. The depot found another role after it passed to the city in 1970. Amtrak’s Desert Wind continued to serve the depot until 1997, after the city took ownership. It now houses city hall, a library and an art gallery, keeping the former railroad building in civic use.
